title: Trauma & the Freeze Response
hook: When escape seems impossible, bodies sometimes stop moving altogether, and the stillness that follows is not calm, consent or indifference.
why:
Most people know the phrase *fight or flight*. Fewer know that bodies have other answers to danger, and that one of the most common is to stop moving. People freeze in assaults, accidents, attacks and disasters, often to their own lasting shame, because they believe they should have fought or run. Afterwards, many carry their bodies differently for months or years: jumping at noises, scanning rooms, sitting with their backs to the wall, going suddenly still when something reminds them of what happened.

This chapter teaches you to recognise those responses and to respond in ways that help rather than harm. You will learn the full range of the body's defences, why freezing is not a choice, what life looks like when the body's alarm stays on, how reminders can pull the past into the present, the habits that make you safer company for someone who has been through trauma, why you should never make anyone tell their story, and the encouraging fact that treatment works. Nothing here is a way to diagnose anyone. It is a way to be a safe person to be near.

teach.h: Bodies have more than two answers to danger.
teach.p:
In 2015 Kasia Kozlowska and colleagues reviewed what is known about the body's defence responses across animals and humans, and described them as a cascade. When a threat appears, the first response is arousal: the body becomes alert and orients towards the danger. If action seems possible, the next is fight or flight. Freezing, in this account, is a state of alert stillness in which fight or flight is put on hold: the body is primed to move but holds still, perhaps to avoid being noticed, while it assesses what to do.

If escape seems impossible and the threat is overwhelming, the cascade can go further. Tonic immobility is a last-resort state in which the body becomes unable to move or speak, sometimes rigid, while the person remains aware of what is happening. Collapsed immobility goes further still: muscle tone is lost and the person may faint or become barely conscious. Kozlowska and colleagues describe these later responses as involuntary, driven by ancient brain systems rather than by any decision.

For a reader, the cascade explains behaviour that otherwise seems baffling. A man who went completely still when he was attacked, a woman who could not scream, a child who went limp, a soldier who froze under fire: none of them chose it, and none of them failed. Their bodies did what bodies do when the threat seems too great for fighting or running.

It also explains why stillness in the face of threat can be so easily misread, by observers, by courts, and by the people themselves.

Fight and flight are not the only options the body has. Sometimes the body chooses stillness, and the person is not consulted.
teach.disconfirm: If people facing overwhelming threat always fought or fled, with freezing and immobility rare, the cascade would describe animals more than humans. The research on human responses to assault and disaster, including the study described next, found immobility to be common.
teach.pullQuote: Sometimes the body chooses stillness, and the person is not consulted.

teach.p:
In 2017 Anna Möller, Hans Peter Söndergaard and Lotti Helström studied women who came to an emergency clinic in Stockholm after a sexual assault. They asked about tonic immobility during the assault: whether the women had felt unable to move or cry out despite wanting to. Of nearly three hundred women, around seven in ten reported significant immobility, and almost half reported extreme immobility. Those who had experienced it were more likely to develop post-traumatic stress and severe depression in the months afterwards.

The study involved women, but the same response occurs in men during assaults, robberies and other violence. Many male survivors describe the same shame: *why didn't I do anything?*

The findings matter for three reasons. First, they show that freezing during an assault is common, not unusual. Second, they show that it is involuntary, which means that a person who froze did not consent, did not cooperate and did not fail. The chapter on touch made the same point: stillness is not a yes. Third, they show that freezing is linked to later distress, partly because survivors so often blame themselves for it.

For a reader, the practical consequence is simple and important. Never ask someone who has been assaulted why they did not fight back, and never read their stillness at the time as agreement. If they blame themselves for freezing, you can tell them, truthfully, that freezing is one of the body's most common responses to overwhelming danger, and that it is not a choice.

Stillness under threat is a defence, not a decision.
teach.disconfirm: If people who froze during assaults turned out, when asked carefully, to have been able to move and to have chosen not to, the involuntary account would be wrong. The research on tonic immobility, and survivors' own accounts, describe the opposite.

teach.h: After trauma, the alarm can stay on.
teach.p:
After a frightening event, most people are shaken for a while: sleep is broken, the event replays in their mind, they feel on edge. For many, this settles over weeks. For some, it does not, and the body behaves as though the danger is still present.

The signs are often visible to the people around them. Hypervigilance: scanning rooms on entering, checking exits, sitting with the back to a wall, watching the door. An exaggerated startle: a dropped pan or a slammed door produces a jump, a flinch or a sudden stillness out of all proportion. Irritability and a short fuse. Poor sleep and nightmares. Avoidance of places, people or activities connected to what happened: the high street where the attack took place, driving after a crash, crowds after a terror attack. Some people seem numb or far away, as if part of them has switched off.

When these persist for more than about a month and disrupt life, clinicians may assess for post-traumatic stress disorder. That assessment belongs to a doctor or psychologist, not to you. But the signs are worth recognising, because they are often misread: the jumpy man as nervous, the irritable man as bad-tempered, the man who will not go into town as stubborn.

It helps to understand these behaviours as the body's learned protection. After a threat, the alarm system has been retuned to fire earlier and louder. That is exhausting to live with, and it is not weakness.

An alarm that keeps ringing is not a fault in the person. It is a body still trying to keep them safe.
teach.disconfirm: If people after frightening events showed no more scanning, startle or avoidance than anyone else, the account in this block would be wrong. Most people who have been through a serious frightening event recognise at least some of these changes in the weeks afterwards.

teach.h: Reminders can pull the past into the present.
teach.p:
For someone whose alarm is still tuned to a past danger, a reminder can bring that danger into the present with startling force. Reminders can be obvious, such as fireworks for a former soldier or a car horn for a crash survivor, or subtle: a smell, a tone of voice, a particular aftershave, being touched from behind, a crowded room, a raised voice, the time of year.

The response may look like any part of the defence cascade. A sudden freeze, the person going rigid and silent. A panic, with the breathing described in the chapter on breath. An angry outburst that seems to come from nowhere. Or a kind of absence, eyes glazed, the person not quite there, sometimes called dissociation. Afterwards the person may be exhausted, embarrassed or unaware of how long they were gone.

If you are with someone when this happens, the aim is to help them come back to the present. Speak calmly and use their name. Tell them where they are and that they are safe: *Sam. It's me. We're in the kitchen. It's Tuesday. You're safe.* Do not grab or touch them without asking; touch may feel like part of the threat. Give them space and a clear way out. Invite them to notice the room: the feel of the chair, their feet on the floor, something they can see.

Afterwards, do not demand an explanation. A simple *Are you all right? Do you want anything?* is enough. If they want to tell you what happened, listen.

When the past breaks into the present, your calm voice is a bridge back.
teach.disconfirm: If people having a reminder-triggered reaction were helped just as much by being touched or questioned as by calm words, space and grounding in the present, this block's advice would not matter. Survivors' accounts and clinical guidance consistently favour the calmer approach.

teach.p:
In 2014 the United States Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration set out six principles for what it called a trauma-informed approach: safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; and attention to cultural, historical and gender issues. They were written for organisations, but they translate into everyday habits that make you safer company for anyone who has been through something frightening, whether or not you know about it.

Safety: notice how people arrange themselves, and let someone sit where they can see the door if they want to. Approach from the front, where you can be seen, rather than from behind. Trustworthiness and transparency: say what you are going to do before you do it. *I'm going to open the window.* *I'm just going to reach past you for the salt.* Do what you said you would do.

Choice and voice: offer choices wherever you can, and respect the answer. Ask before touching, always. Do not insist on hugs, closeness or particular seats. Collaboration: do things with people rather than to them. Peer support: some people find most help from others who have been through something similar, such as other veterans or other survivors. And cultural and historical awareness: some people carry trauma that belongs to their community's history as well as their own.

None of this requires you to know someone's history, and none of it costs you anything. It simply removes the small surprises, losses of control and uninvited touches that can set off an alarm that is still ringing.
teach.disconfirm: If explaining your actions, offering choices and asking before touch made no difference to how at ease people with a history of trauma felt with you, these habits would add nothing. Ask someone you know who has been through a frightening experience whether such things matter to them.

teach.h: Never make anyone tell their story.
teach.p:
When someone has been through something terrible, the instinct of many friends is to get them to talk about it, on the theory that talking will help it heal. Sometimes it does. But pressing someone to describe a traumatic event before they are ready can do harm.

For many years, emergency services and employers offered single-session psychological debriefing to people soon after a traumatic event, in which they were encouraged to go through what happened and their feelings about it. Reviews of the research found that it did not prevent later problems, and in some studies the people who had been debriefed did worse. Clinical guidelines now advise against routine debriefing of this kind. What helps in the early days is practical support, safety, rest and company, with talking available when the person chooses it.

The same applies in everyday life. Let the person decide whether, when and how much to tell you. If they do talk, listen without pressing for details, without questioning their account, and without asking why they did or did not do something. Believe them. Do not compare it with your own experiences, and do not tell their story to others.

If they choose not to talk, that is not a failure of trust. Your steady presence, practical help and patience may matter more than any conversation. Many survivors say that the people who helped most were the ones who simply stayed, and treated them normally.

Let them hold the story. Your job is to hold the space.
teach.disconfirm: If people pressed to describe traumatic events soon afterwards did better over time than people left to talk at their own pace, the advice in this block would be wrong. The reviews of early psychological debriefing found the opposite.

teach.p:
It is worth ending on the most hopeful fact in this chapter. Many people recover from frightening experiences on their own, with time, support and ordinary life. For those who do not, effective treatments exist. Clinical guidelines in many countries recommend trauma-focused psychological therapies, such as trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, for post-traumatic stress, and many people improve substantially with them, even years after the event.

So the most useful thing you can do, when someone's alarm has stayed on for more than about a month, when they are avoiding large parts of life, sleeping badly, drinking to cope, or struggling at work or at home, is to encourage them to see a doctor, and to make it practical. Many countries also have specialist services for veterans, for emergency workers and for survivors of assault, which people can often contact directly.

If the person talks about not wanting to go on, or you are worried for their safety, ask them directly whether they are thinking about suicide, and use the crisis resources in this app. Trauma raises that risk, and asking is safe.

And look after yourself. Hearing about traumatic events, or living alongside someone whose alarm is always on, takes a toll. It is ordinary to need support yourself, and getting it makes you a better support for them.

The body that learned to freeze can learn to feel safe again. Help makes it more likely.
teach.disconfirm: If people with persistent post-traumatic stress improved just as much without treatment as with trauma-focused therapy, encouraging professional help would add little. The evidence behind clinical guidelines suggests treatment helps many people substantially.

poseGallery.doCaption: 'Freezing is the body's response. It wasn't a choice.'
poseGallery.annotation: Tonic immobility is common and involuntary. Asking why someone did not fight adds blame to harm.

poseGallery.doCaption: Approaching where he can see you, and saying his name.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Coming up behind him and touching his shoulder.
poseGallery.annotation: After trauma, surprises and touch from behind can set off an alarm that is still ringing. Be seen, and be heard first.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting him choose whether, when and how much to say.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Pressing him to tell you everything that happened.
poseGallery.annotation: Pressing people to describe trauma early can do harm. Practical support and patience help more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Seeing a body still trying to keep him safe, and staying.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading his jumpiness and short temper as weakness.
poseGallery.annotation: Hypervigilance, startle and irritability are the body's learned protection after a threat, not a flaw.

caseStudy:
Chris, thirty-one, shares a flat with his friend Jamal, thirty-three. In October, Jamal is attacked and robbed on his way home from the station. He is bruised but not badly injured, and tells Chris he is fine. He goes back to work after a week.

Over the next month Chris notices changes. Jamal now walks home the long way, avoiding the high street. In the pub he takes the seat facing the door and keeps glancing at it. When a glass smashes behind the bar, he jumps so hard he spills his drink, then goes very quiet. He is short-tempered, which is not like him, and Chris hears him moving around the flat at three in the morning.

One evening Chris comes up behind Jamal in the kitchen and puts a hand on his shoulder to reach for a mug. Jamal goes rigid, then spins round with his fists up. He stares at Chris for a moment without seeming to see him. Chris steps back and says calmly, *Jamal. It's me. You're at home. You're safe.* After a few seconds Jamal lowers his hands, apologises, and sits down, shaking.

Chris does not ask what happened in October. He says he is sorry for startling him, and that from now on he will say something when he comes into a room. A few days later, on a walk, Jamal tells him a little about the attack: that he froze, could not shout, and has been furious with himself ever since. Chris tells him that freezing is one of the body's most common responses to danger, and not a choice.

In December, when the jumpiness and the broken sleep have not eased, Chris suggests he see his doctor and offers to go with him. Jamal is referred for trauma-focused therapy. By spring he is walking down the high street again, on good days.
observe: Notice how people arrange themselves in a room you enter: who sits facing the door, who takes the seat by the exit.
Notice your own habits of approach: whether you tend to come up behind people, touch without warning, or act without saying what you are about to do.
Notice how people around you react to a sudden loud noise, and how long it takes each of them to return to baseline.

drills.name: Announce Yourself
steps: For one day, say what you are about to do before you do it, whenever it involves someone else's space.
Approach people from where they can see you, rather than from behind.
Ask before any touch, however small.
Notice whether anyone responds differently from usual.
Write down which of these felt most unnatural to you, and why.

drills.name: Grounding Script
steps: Write a short script for helping someone come back to the present: their name, who you are, where they are, the day, that they are safe.
Add two invitations to notice the room, such as their feet on the floor or something they can see.
Say the script aloud slowly until it feels natural.
Note what you would not do: grab, question, crowd.
Keep the script where you can find it.

drills.name: Choice Audit
steps: Think of a setting you control, such as your home, your team meetings or a regular social event.
List the moments where people have no choice, such as where to sit, whether to speak or whether to be touched.
For each, write one way you could offer a choice.
Introduce one of these changes this week.
Note how people respond.

drills.name: Words That Blame
steps: Write down any questions or phrases you might instinctively use with someone after a frightening event, such as why didn't you or you should have.
Mark each that implies they could or should have acted differently.
Write a replacement for each that conveys belief and support.
Write one true sentence you could say to someone who blames themselves for freezing.
Practise saying it aloud.

drills.name: Know the Routes
steps: Find out how someone where you live can be referred for trauma-focused therapy, through a doctor or directly.
Find any specialist services for veterans, emergency workers or survivors of assault in your area.
Find the crisis resources in this app for your region.
Write two practical offers you could make to someone who needs help.
Keep these notes where you can find them quickly.

quiz.q: During a frightening assault, a man froze and could not fight back or shout. What does the research on freezing suggest?
options: That he was too weak or too frightened to protect himself properly
That he must, at some level, have been willing to go along with it
That freezing is an involuntary defence; it says nothing of consent or courage
That he was in shock and will not remember anything about what happened
quiz.explain: Tonic immobility is a last-resort defence driven by ancient brain systems, not a decision. It is common, and survivors often blame themselves for it, which adds to their distress. It tells you nothing about consent or courage.

quiz.q: In Möller and colleagues' study of women seen at a clinic after sexual assault, roughly how many reported significant tonic immobility?
options: About seven in ten
About one in ten
Almost none of them
Only those who were injured
quiz.explain: Around seventy percent reported significant immobility and nearly half extreme immobility, and those who froze were more likely to develop post-traumatic stress and severe depression. Freezing is common, not rare.

quiz.q: In the defence cascade described by Kozlowska and colleagues, what is tonic immobility?
options: A deliberate decision to stay still so as not to be noticed by an attacker
A form of fainting caused by low blood sugar during a stressful situation
A trained response that soldiers and police learn in order to stay calm
An involuntary, last-resort immobility when escape seems impossible
quiz.explain: It comes after arousal, fight or flight and alert freezing, when the threat seems overwhelming. The person cannot move or cry out, often while fully aware, and does not choose it.

quiz.q: Since being mugged, your friend jumps at sudden noises and sits with his back to the wall. You need to wake him from a nap on the sofa. What fits?
options: Shake his shoulder firmly so that he wakes up quickly and fully
Call his name from the doorway, where he can see you, before you approach
Creep in quietly so as not to startle him, then tap him gently
Let him sleep on, since waking him is likely to upset him whatever you do
quiz.explain: After a threat, surprise and touch can set off an alarm that is still on. Being seen and heard first, from a little distance, lets him wake into safety rather than into a reminder.

quiz.q: Which of these fits a trauma-informed approach in everyday life?
options: Insisting on a hug to show you care, even if they hesitate at first
Encouraging them to describe what happened in detail straight away
Saying what you will do before you do it, and offering choices
Treating them as fragile, and making all of their decisions for them
quiz.explain: Transparency and choice restore some of the control that trauma takes away. Insisting on touch, pressing for the story and taking over decisions all remove control again.

quiz.q: Two months after a serious car crash, a colleague still has nightmares, avoids driving and is constantly on edge. What fits this chapter?
options: Encourage him to see a doctor, since trauma-focused therapies help many
Tell him it has been long enough and that he needs to get back behind the wheel
Ask him to tell you exactly what happened, since talking about it will help
Leave it, since these things always settle down on their own in the end
quiz.explain: Signs that persist beyond a month and disrupt life are a reason to seek help, and effective treatments exist. Pushing him to drive or to tell the story can make things worse; making a doctor's appointment practical helps.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you know who has been through a frightening experience: an accident, an assault, combat, a disaster, a violent home. What, if anything, changed in how they carried their body afterwards: how they sat, how they reacted to noise, where they would and would not go? How did people around them read those changes? Then think about your own habits: which of the trauma-informed habits in this chapter would make you safer company for them, and which will you practise this week?
reflection.guidance: You do not need to know the details of what happened to answer this, and you should not seek them out. Focus on what was visible and on how it was read. Many people realise that someone they thought of as jumpy or short-tempered was carrying something heavy. The habit you choose should be concrete: announcing yourself, asking before touch, offering a choice.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read freezing as consent, weakness or willingness, and to ask a survivor why they did not fight. The second is to misread the after-effects of trauma, treating hypervigilance as paranoia, startle as nervousness and irritability as bad temper. The third is to set off the alarm by accident: coming up from behind, touching without asking, making sudden moves, surprising someone who cannot bear surprise. The fourth is to press for the story, believing that talking always heals, when pressing early can harm. And the fifth is to leave it too long, waiting for signs that have lasted months to settle on their own. Be predictable, offer choice, ask before touch, believe people, and help them reach treatment that works.
